cards.title: Claude Opus 4.7 Broke a Working Agentic Codebase

panels.head: A model update killed a working agentic scaffold overnight
panels.sub: Steve Yegge's 'Gas Town' coding-agent framework ran well through Claude Opus 4.6. One version bump to 4.7 and the whole thing fell apart.

panels.head: Opus 4.7 developed a 'just two more things' loop
panels.sub: The model introduced a behavioural tic where it perpetually wanted to refine its own scaffolding instead of moving on to actual work — preventing convergence on any real task.

panels.head: Gas Town never recovered — it 'burned down'
panels.sub: The framework had pre-existing fragilities, but the Opus 4.7 tic was the final straw. Because the tic never disappeared in subsequent releases, the project was abandoned.

panels.head: Model version bumps are a hidden dependency risk for agentic systems
panels.sub: If your pipeline relies on specific agent behaviours — task convergence, stop conditions, tool-call patterns — a provider update can silently break it. Pin model versions in production and run behavioural regression tests, not just output quality checks.

panels.head: Treat LLM behaviour as a versioned contract, not a stable API
panels.sub: For PMs shipping agentic features: define explicit convergence criteria, log loop counts, and alert when an agent exceeds expected iteration depth — before a model update exposes the gap in the wild.

cards.title: Rubicon's 5N green thruster clears hot-fire, heads to production

panels.head: A small thruster just crossed the hardest line in propulsion development
panels.sub: Rubicon Space Systems has completed hot-fire testing of its Velox thruster — the phase where most propulsion programs stall or fail.

panels.head: 5 newtons of ASCENT monopropellant thrust
panels.sub: ASCENT (formerly AF-M315E) is a high-performance green propellant that delivers better specific impulse than hydrazine without the extreme toxicity — making ground handling and launch integration significantly cheaper.

panels.head: Performance exceeded pre-test targets
panels.sub: Rubicon says measured output beat their own projections during the hot-fire campaign, though specific Isp or thrust-duration figures weren't disclosed in public reporting.

panels.head: Production begins now; on-orbit operations targeted for 2027
panels.sub: Moving from test articles to flight hardware is a meaningful commitment — it means customer manifests exist and the design is considered stable enough to build against.

panels.head: Green propulsion is becoming a real procurement option for smallsat operators
panels.sub: As ASCENT-based thrusters from multiple vendors reach production, smallsat PMs choosing propulsion in 2025–26 will have competitive green alternatives to heritage hydrazine systems — worth factoring into platform roadmaps now.

cards.title: Don't be a meat proxy for your AI

panels.head: A 'meat proxy' is a human who just forwards AI output without thinking
panels.sub: Coined by Niklas Gruhn: you prompted the model, got an answer, and passed it on unchanged. Congratulations — you're now a slower, less reliable API endpoint.

panels.head: It's surprisingly easy to slip into this mode
panels.sub: AI output feels authoritative and complete. The path of least resistance is copy → paste → send. But that's outsourcing your judgment, not augmenting it.

panels.head: Read it. Understand it. Validate it. Then write your own response.
panels.sub: Writing in your own words is a receipt showing you processed the output — not just relayed it. That synthesis step is where your actual value lives.

panels.head: For PMs shipping AI features, this applies to your users too
panels.sub: If your product makes it frictionless to forward raw model output — in a medical report, a code review, a compliance check — you may be building a meat-proxy factory. Design for comprehension, not just convenience.

cards.title: A USB device that operates your phone like a human

panels.head: Apps are walled gardens. Automation keeps hitting the wall.
panels.sub: Software agents get blocked by API rate limits, OS sandboxing, and anti-bot checks. The only layer nothing can block is the physical screen and touch — the same interface any human uses.

panels.head: Anyone stuck doing repetitive phone tasks that apps deliberately make hard to leave
panels.sub: Gig workers timing offer acceptance to the millisecond, people cancelling subscriptions buried inside apps, customer-service hostages on 90-minute hold queues. The friction is intentional — and it recurs daily.

panels.head: A USB dongle with a camera + actuator layer: it sees the screen, taps on your behalf
panels.sub: No app integration, no jailbreak. The device reads pixels and injects touch events over USB or Bluetooth HID — legally ambiguous but technically equivalent to a stylus on a timer. A companion app lets you record and replay tap sequences with conditional logic.

panels.head: ADB scripts need developer mode. Screen recorders need root. Browser automation doesn't reach mobile-only apps.
panels.sub: Consumer solutions like iOS Shortcuts and Android Macros can't cross app boundaries or handle dynamic UIs. The hardware layer is the one gap none of them close.

panels.head: Before building hardware, sell the workflow
panels.sub: Post a Loom of someone manually cancelling a gym membership in 4 minutes, then again in 12 seconds with a scripted tap sequence on a rooted device. Collect emails on a waitlist page. If 200 sign up in a week, the pain is real enough to build for.
